english_translation: Women used to go to the well to fetch water while sharing their stories with one another.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('Vakadzi')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'Vakadzi' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('kunotora')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'kunotora' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('dzavo')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'dzavo' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).

cultural_notes.title: The Village Well ('Tsime') as a Space of Fellowship and Storytelling
cultural_notes.content: In rural communities, walking together to fetch cool water from the village spring or well ('kutsime') was a cherished daily social hour where women shared news, advice, and laughter along the footpath.

active_exercises.prompt: How do you say 'Tall trees and green grass' in Shona?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Miti mirefu' = 'tall trees' (plural 'mi-' agreement on '-refu'), and 'neuswa hwegirinhi' = 'and green grass'.

active_exercises.prompt: In 'Shiri diki dziri kuimba pamusoro pemuti', what are the small birds doing?
options: Singing at the top of the tree
Looking for seeds in the field
active_exercises.correct_answer: Singing at the top of the tree
active_exercises.explanation: 'Shiri diki' = 'small birds', 'dziri kuimba' = 'are singing', 'pamusoro pemuti' = 'at the top of the tree'.

active_exercises.prompt: If a friend asks you in the afternoon 'Waswera sei?', what is the natural reply?
active_exercises.explanation: In Shona, you reply to 'Waswera sei?' ('How did you spend the day?') with 'Ndaswera kana waswerawo' ('I spent the day well if you spent it well too').
